body.heading: A modern puzzle with a long passport
paragraphs: The Sudoku we know was published in 1979 by American puzzle maker Howard Garns under the name Number Place. It travelled to Japan in the 1980s, where the publisher Nikoli named it Sudoku — roughly, “the digits must remain single” — and from Japan it conquered the world's newspapers.
The rules fit in one breath: fill the nine-by-nine grid so that every row, column and three-by-three box contains the digits 1 to 9 exactly once. Everything else is technique.

body.heading: Scan, don't guess
paragraphs: The core technique is scanning. Pick a number, say 7, and look at the rows and columns that already contain a 7: each one rules out a whole line of the box you are studying. Where the ruled-out lines leave a single cell standing, that cell must be the 7.

Work through the grid number by number, then start again — every placed digit creates new exclusions. If scanning stalls, pencil in candidates: the small possible digits for each empty cell. A cell with only one candidate is solved; a pair of cells sharing the same two candidates locks those digits away from the rest of the row.

body.heading: Try it: the two-minute drill
paragraphs: Take an easy puzzle and set one rule for yourself: no guessing, and every placement must be explained aloud — “this must be 4 because...” Explaining slows you down for one puzzle and speeds you up for every puzzle after.
Then try solving cooperatively: two solvers, one grid, taking turns to place a number and justify it. Sudoku is a solo game that secretly loves company.

takeaway: Sudoku is not about being good at numbers; it is about eliminating the impossible until only the truth is left.
